title: How to Enable Cross-Origin Requests (CORS) in ASP.NET Core
description: Enable and configure CORS in ASP.NET Core applications using the built-in middleware.

data.text: What You Will Build

By the end of this lesson, your ASP.NET Core API will accept cross-origin requests from specific frontend domains. You will configure CORS in two ways: a simple global policy and a more structured named policy.

data.title: Prerequisites
data.text: This lesson assumes you have a working ASP.NET Core Web API project and understand what the same-origin policy is. If you are new to CORS, complete the 'Understanding CORS and the Same-Origin Policy' lesson first.
Two-Step Setup
Enabling CORS in ASP.NET Core requires two steps in Program.cs. First, you register the CORS service. Second, you add the CORS middleware to the request pipeline.

data.title: Steps to Enable CORS
items: Call builder.Services.AddCors() in the service registration section.
Call app.UseCors() in the middleware pipeline, between UseRouting and UseAuthorization.

data.text: Example: Simple Global CORS Policy
Below is a minimal Program.cs that allows any origin, any method, and any header. This is useful for local testing but should not be used in production.

data.title: Program.cs — Basic Global CORS
data.content: Add CORS services and middleware to allow all origins, methods, and headers.

data.title: Development Only
data.text: AllowAnyOrigin() opens your API to every website. Use it only during local development. In production, always switch to WithOrigins() with explicit domain names.
Restricting to Specific Origins
Replace AllowAnyOrigin() with WithOrigins() to limit which domains can call your API. The origins must include the scheme (https://) and no trailing slash.

data.title: Program.cs — Allow Specific Origins
data.content: Restrict CORS to one trusted frontend domain.

data.text: You can pass multiple origins as a string array. This is useful when your API serves a web app, a mobile app backend, and an admin dashboard.

data.title: Program.cs — Allow Multiple Origins
data.content: Allow three different trusted domains to access the API.

data.text: Key CORS Policy Methods

rows: Allow every domain to access the API
Allow GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, and all other methods
Allow only the listed HTTP methods
Allow any request header the client sends
Allow only the listed request headers
Allow cookies or Authorization headers in cross-origin requests
Control how long the browser caches the preflight result

data.text: Apply CORS Per Controller or Per Action
A global UseCors policy applies to every endpoint. For finer control, define a named policy with AddPolicy and apply it using the [EnableCors] attribute on controllers or actions.

data.title: Program.cs — Named Policy Definition
data.content: Define a policy called 'AdminPolicy' that only allows the admin frontend.

data.text: Per Action
Place [EnableCors("PolicyName")] directly above the action method. The action overrides any controller-level policy.

data.title: Controller — Action-Level CORS
data.content: Enable the AdminPolicy only on a specific action.

data.text: Per Controller
Place [EnableCors("PolicyName")] above the controller class. Every action inherits this policy unless an action overrides it.

data.title: Controller — Controller-Level CORS
data.content: Apply a policy to all actions in a controller.

data.text: Disabling CORS
Use [DisableCors] on an action or controller when you want to block cross-origin access for that specific endpoint, even if a global or controller-level policy exists.

data.title: Controller — Disabling CORS
data.content: Block cross-origin access to a single action.

data.title: Enable CORS in a New Project
data.description: Practice enabling CORS in a brand-new ASP.NET Core Web API project.
steps: Create a new ASP.NET Core Web API project.
Add a simple GET endpoint at /api/values that returns a string array.
Register a global CORS policy that allows https://localhost:3000.
Place app.UseCors() in the correct position in the middleware pipeline.
Run the API and use curl or a browser fetch() from another origin to verify CORS is working.
data.expectedOutcome: A working API that accepts cross-origin requests from https://localhost:3000 and rejects requests from other origins.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Apply CORS middleware with app.UseCors() between UseRouting and UseAuthorization
Use WithOrigins() to restrict access to specific domains
Use [EnableCors] on controllers or actions for fine-grained control
Use [DisableCors] to block cross-origin access for a specific endpoint
data.takeaway: You now know how to enable CORS in ASP.NET Core. Next, you will learn about named policies and how to apply them selectively.
